title: Ganglion Cyst: A Lump on the Wrist or Hand — Does It Need Removing?
metaDescription: A soft lump on the wrist is usually a harmless ganglion cyst. When to leave it, whether draining helps, when surgery makes sense and how often it comes back.
intro: A smooth, rubbery lump on the back or front of the wrist is one of the most common reasons people come to a hand clinic. Most of these are ganglion cysts. They can look alarming, but they are not cancer, many disappear on their own, and a large number never need any treatment at all. The real questions are whether yours is a ganglion, and whether it is causing enough trouble to be worth treating.

sections.heading: What is a ganglion cyst?
sections.body: A ganglion cyst is a fluid-filled sac that grows out of a joint or tendon sheath, which AAOS describes as being like a balloon on a stalk. It is not cancerous. Common sites are the back of the wrist (the most typical place), the palm side of the wrist, the base of a finger and the fingertip. Ganglions are most common between the ages of 15 and 40, and in women more than men. They vary in size from smaller than a pea to a few centimetres across.

sections.heading: Is it painful, and can it damage my hand?
sections.body: Usually it is painless, apart from a visible lump. Some cysts ache during or after moving the wrist, and a cyst that presses on a nearby nerve can cause tingling or weakness. AAOS notes that ganglions rarely, if ever, cause permanent disability. Some smaller ganglions stay hidden under the skin and are only found on a scan.

sections.heading: Will a ganglion cyst go away on its own?
sections.body: Often, yes. AAOS states that more than half go away on their own, and the NHS says they usually improve without treatment, although this can take several months up to a year. That is why, for a lump that does not hurt or interfere with your hand, watching it is a safe and sensible first choice. A wrist splint may ease symptoms if it aches, and sometimes the cyst shrinks while the wrist is rested.

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.body: In most cases a doctor can diagnose a ganglion simply by examining it. Because it is filled with fluid, light shone against it usually passes through. An ultrasound can confirm a fluid-filled cyst with clear borders, and an MRI is very accurate at finding small hidden cysts. An X-ray does not show the cyst itself, but may be taken to look for arthritis in the nearby joint. A lump that is hard, fixed, growing quickly or not behaving like a ganglion should be properly assessed rather than assumed to be one.

sections.heading: Should I have it drained, or removed with surgery?
sections.body: Treatment is only worth considering if the cyst is painful, limits your hand, presses on a nerve or genuinely bothers you. Draining it with a needle (aspiration) is quick and low-risk, but it often comes back. Surgical removal of the cyst and its stalk is more likely to last, but it carries more risk and recovery time, and even then the cyst can return. sections.heading: What do those numbers mean for me?
sections.body: Aspiration is a reasonable first step for many people because it is simple and safe, as long as you accept a better-than-even chance that the lump returns. Surgery lowers the chance of recurrence compared with aspiration. The keyhole figures look best, but the same review noted that comparative trials are limited and have not shown keyhole surgery to be clearly superior. After surgery, AAOS states that most people return to normal activities within 2 to 6 weeks.

sections.heading: Can I burst it at home, or hit it with a book?
sections.body: No. The old advice to hit a ganglion with a heavy book can injure your hand and is unlikely to get rid of the cyst, according to AAOS. The NHS also warns against trying to burst or pop a ganglion yourself, because it can cause infection or damage the skin. If it hurts, rest, a wrist support and simple anti-inflammatory painkillers, if you can safely take them, are the sensible steps until it is assessed.

sections.heading: When should I get a lump on my hand checked?
sections.body: Have any new lump checked if you are worried about it, if it is getting bigger, or if it is hard and does not move. A lump that is very painful, hot or red should be seen promptly, as that is not typical of a ganglion and may mean infection or inflammation. Tingling, numbness or weakness in the fingers alongside a lump is also worth an early assessment.

faqs.a: No. A ganglion cyst is a harmless fluid-filled sac arising from a joint or tendon sheath. A lump that is hard, fixed in place, growing or not behaving like a typical ganglion should still be examined to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Will a ganglion cyst go away without treatment?
faqs.a: Often, yes. More than half disappear on their own, though it can take several months up to a year. If it does not hurt or limit your hand, watching it is a safe first choice.

faqs.q: Does draining a ganglion cyst work?
faqs.a: It can, but it often comes back. In a 2015 review of published studies, ganglions recurred after about 59% of needle aspirations, compared with about 21% after open surgical removal.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after ganglion surgery?
faqs.a: Ganglion removal is usually a day procedure. According to AAOS, most people return to normal activities within 2 to 6 weeks. The cyst can still come back after surgery, though less often than after draining.

faqs.q: Can I pop a ganglion cyst at home?
faqs.a: No. Trying to burst it, or hitting it with a book, can injure your hand or cause infection and is unlikely to get rid of the cyst.
